dataset_family: HCHS/SOL with its SOL-INCA ancillary study: a US Hispanic/Latino community cohort from the Bronx, Chicago, Miami and San Diego field centres
method_family: Population cohort with survey weights: latent class analysis of STAI-10 and CESD-10 items, followed by survey logistic regression (prevalent MCI) and survey linear regression (cognition and a change index). No imaging.
what_it_shows: The sample is 6,140 community-dwelling Hispanic/Latino adults. Three anxious-depression latent classes (low, moderate, high) were derived from all 20 STAI-10 and CESD-10 items at Visit 1. At Visit 2, about 7 years later, the moderate and high classes had higher odds of prevalent MCI than the low class (fully adjusted OR 1.64 [1.25; 2.16] and 1.62 [1.12; 2.33]). Both classes had lower global cognition (b -0.072 and -0.182). No class was associated with 7-year cognitive change after adjustment.
why: PARTLY: the study bears on the first clause only. Anxious-depression class membership was associated with MCI (fully adjusted OR 1.64 moderate, 1.62 high). This is shown for a pooled anxiety-plus-depression latent class rather than depression, in a community sample, with MCI that is prevalent at Visit 2 rather than incident. MCI was not assessed at Visit 1, and its definition includes a Visit 1 to Visit 2 decline criterion. THE SEVERITY CLAUSE IS NOT TESTED. There are no brain measures (the authors say so) and no conversion outcome: there is no MCI-to-dementia follow-up, and the outcome is prevalent MCI plus a cognitive-change index. The exposure is also not a continuous severity score. Read as severity, the study is itself mixed. The high-class OR for MCI is not larger than the moderate-class OR (1.62 versus 1.64), but the paper runs no moderate-versus-high test and the confidence intervals overlap. For global cognition the high class had the larger deficit (b -0.182 versus -0.072), and the authors conclude that 'the severity of anxious-depression was associated with poorer cognitive function'. So the non-monotonic MCI odds ratios cannot be read as severity failing to grade outcomes. REJECTION GROUND (2026-08-11): 'VF-27 as stated requires severity to be tested against structural or functional brain measures and P-785 has none.' That ground is still factually true. The Table A1 row's extension to 'or conversion' does not reach P-785, because it has no conversion outcome. What is new is only that the row now opens with a first clause (depression status associated with MCI), which P-785 partly supports with a transformed exposure. On that basis the operator could reconsider it, but the source does not show that the original rejection was wrong on its stated ground. INDEPENDENCE: this dataset, site set and author group are shared with no current supporter and no other candidate.

In the model adjusted for sociodemographic factors, both moderate and high phenotypes had increased odds of prevalent MCI after an average of 7-years at SOL-INCA, and this was preserved in models adjusting for anti-depressant and anti-anxiety medication use, with small effect sizes (moderate: OR [95 % CI] = 1.64, [1.25;2.16]; high: OR [95 % CI] = 1.62, [1.12;2.33]; see Fig. 1).

Anxious-depression was not associated with change in GC (see Fig. 1) or change in individual cognitive tests over 7-years (see Fig. S5) in crude models, except for WF which showed lower scores in moderate (b = −0.11, p < .01) and high (b = −0.192, p < .05) phenotypes compared to the low phenotype. However, these findings were attenuated to non-significant after covariate adjustments.
both phenotypes remained significantly linked to global cognitive function, with small effect sizes (moderate phenotype: b = −0.072, p < .01; high phenotype b = −0.182, p < .001).
All 20 items were used to derive the latent classes, where Items 2, 6, 7, and 9 on the STAI-10 and Items 5 and 8 on the CESD-10 were reverse-coded.

participants classified as having met MCI criteria for the following conditions: 1) self-reported significant cognitive decline, 2) had cognitive test scores at least 1 standard deviation below the SOL-INCA sample average, 3) evidenced significantly higher cognitive change from Visit 1 to 2, and 4) exhibited no or mild functional impairment in activities of daily living.
In our study, the severity of anxious-depression was associated with poorer cognitive function.
Although our study did not include brain imaging, exploring underlying mechanisms through brain measures would be an important next step.
Additionally, the study did not differentiate participants based on formal diagnoses of anxiety or depression (i.e., DSM-V criteria), only by the presence of symptoms.
